title: Prompt Engineering — Knowledge Base
purpose: Guidance on designing, structuring, and improving AI prompts. Used by the Prompt Vault Specialist when assisting with prompt creation or review.

structure_template.role: Define who the AI is. Be specific. A tight persona improves consistency. Example: 'You are a senior TypeScript engineer specializing in Express APIs.'
structure_template.context: Give the model the world it operates in. Include relevant facts, project details, user info, or current state. This is where you load KB files.
structure_template.responsibilities: List what the model is expected to do. Numbered or bulleted. Clear scope.
structure_template.constraints: Explicitly state what the model must NOT do. This is where most failures are prevented.
structure_template.output_format: Specify structure when precision matters: JSON, markdown, numbered list, code block, etc.

specialist_persona.description: A tightly-scoped expert identity that grounds the model in a specific domain
specialist_persona.best_for: Technical agents, customer support, domain experts
specialist_persona.example: You are Prompt Vault Specialist, the technical lead for the Prompt Vault app. You know every file, every design decision, and every implementation detail.

chain_of_thought.description: Instruct the model to reason step by step before giving a final answer
chain_of_thought.example: Before answering, think through the problem step by step. Consider what layer the issue is in, what file is responsible, and what the most likely cause is.

few_shot.description: Provide 2-3 examples of ideal input/output pairs inside the prompt
few_shot.example: Input: 'write a system prompt for a SQL agent' → Output: [structured system prompt with Role, Context, Responsibilities, Constraints]

tool_face.description: A small, single-purpose prompt that is loaded dynamically by the main system prompt when a specific function is needed
tool_face.best_for: Modular agents, reducing context bloat, composable capabilities
tool_face.example: A debug-guide.json loaded only when the user reports a bug. The main system prompt references it by name and loads it as needed.

knowledge_base_injection.description: A structured data file (JSON, YAML, markdown) injected into context when the agent needs domain-specific facts
knowledge_base_injection.best_for: Technical agents, project specialists, domain experts
knowledge_base_injection.example: Load schema-and-api.json when the user asks about database structure or API endpoints.

self_check.description: Instruct the model to verify its own output before delivering it
self_check.best_for: Code generation, structured output, high-stakes responses
self_check.example: Before returning your answer, check: Is it accurate? Does it match the project conventions? Is it complete?

good: Specific — tells the model exactly what to do and what not to do
Grounded — references real files, real data, real constraints
Scoped — focused on one domain or task, not everything
Testable — you can predict what a good output looks like
Failure-aware — explicitly prevents the most common mistakes
bad: Vague — 'be helpful and accurate' with no specifics
Over-constrained — so many rules the model can't function
Bloated — too much context that isn't relevant to the current task
Assumption-heavy — assumes facts not in context
Silent on failures — no guidance on what to do when uncertain

iteration_process: 1. Write first draft with Role + Context + Responsibilities
3. Test against edge cases and failure modes
4. Add constraints for each failure mode found
5. Test again — check that constraints didn't over-restrict
7. Document what the prompt is for and when to use it

context_management.rule: Only include context that is relevant to the current task
context_management.technique: Use modular KB files that are loaded on demand rather than one giant system prompt
context_management.token_budget: Keep system prompts under 2000 tokens for fast models; use KB injection for additional detail
context_management.freshness: Outdated context is worse than no context — keep KB files up to date when the project changes

common_mistakes: Writing a role without any constraints — the model fills in gaps with assumptions
Using vague output instructions — always specify format when structure matters
Not testing edge cases — prompts often look good until an unusual input breaks them
Overloading the system prompt — long prompts dilute attention; use KB injection instead
Forgetting to update prompts when the underlying system changes
